text: The measures are built and the visuals are in place. This lesson makes the report filterable and makes it read clearly to someone who isn't going to study it — just glance at it.

Even though this report is scoped to one stakeholder, the underlying query returns every territory, kept for context. Add a slicer — drop it from the Visualizations pane, drag Territory into its field well, and choose single selection if the manager only ever looks at one region, or multi-select if they sometimes want two or three compared side by side.

Here's where writing measures back in lesson six pays off directly. Total Sales, Order Count, and Average Order Value are all measures, which means every card, the bar chart, and the table all recalculate automatically the instant the slicer selection changes. No extra wiring, no rebuilding anything — that's the whole point of using measures instead of raw columns.

Now formatting, matched to what each number actually is. Total Sales gets currency formatting with no decimal places — a stakeholder comparing regions doesn't need cents. Order Count gets a plain whole number with a thousands separator — it isn't money. Average Order Value gets currency with two decimal places, since at that smaller scale, cents can actually matter for comparison. Set each format once, on the measure itself, and every visual using it inherits it automatically.

Last piece: titles. A default title just repeats field names — sum of TotalSalesAmount by Territory. Replace it with something that states the answer — Sales by Region. Do the same for the KPI cards and the table. For a report someone glances at once before a call, the title is often the only text they actually read.
The report is filterable, formatted, and titled for its real audience. Next lesson, we publish it from Power BI Desktop to the Power BI Service, so the stakeholder can actually open it.
